explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says, "The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs." (Luke 17:20) No countdown, no flashing arrow, nothing to squint at from the window. The Pharisees asked for a date, and Jesus gave them something else to chew on.

Jesus says the exact opposite, baker. He tells the Pharisees, "The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs." (Luke 17:20) So there's nothing to stand around watching for. I'll be honest, I would have loved a sign too, even a tiny one shaped like a cookie.

Right there with them! Jesus says, "…the kingdom of God is in your midst." (Luke 17:21) The Pharisees were looking all over for it, and Jesus was standing in front of them. That's like hunting the whole kitchen for the spatula while you're holding it.

No desert in this verse, friend. Jesus says people won't be saying, "Look, here it is," or "There it is." Then He says, "…the kingdom of God is in your midst." (Luke 17:21) So the answer is closer than any desert.

Good guess, but Jesus doesn't point to the temple here. He says nobody will be saying, "Look, here it is," or "There it is." He tells the Pharisees, "…the kingdom of God is in your midst." (Luke 17:21) He doesn't name a building at all.

Careful, this one flips on you. Jesus says, "The time is coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it." (Luke 17:22) So they'll long for it, and they won't see it. That's the part I'd read twice.

Yep, false. Jesus tells the disciples, "…you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it." (Luke 17:22) The longing is there, and the seeing is not. It's a quiet line, and I think it's a tender one.
That's what Jesus says, friend. "Do not go out or chase after them." (Luke 17:23) When somebody hollers "Look, there He is!", the disciples stay put. No sprinting, no sneakers, no dust cloud.
Nice teamwork, but Jesus says the opposite. His words are, "Do not go out or chase after them." (Luke 17:23) Going out together is still going out. The group trip is off.

explanations.answer: Send one of them to look
explanations.explanation: Sending a scout sounds smart, I'll give you that. But Jesus says, "Do not go out or chase after them." (Luke 17:23) He doesn't leave a spot for a volunteer. Nobody draws the short straw here.

Bright and unmistakable! Jesus says, "For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day." (Luke 17:24) That's the picture He gives. Lightning doesn't need anybody pointing at it.

explanations.answer: Like a quiet knock at night
explanations.explanation: That's a sweet picture, but it's not the one Jesus uses. He says, "For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day." (Luke 17:24) A flash across the whole sky is about as far from a quiet knock as you can get.

Seeds are a big deal in Jesus' teaching, and Buttercup, one of my cookie cutter kids, would be thrilled you thought of one. But not in this verse. Jesus says, "For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day." (Luke 17:24) Lightning is quick, and it's everywhere at once.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation." (Luke 17:25) He says it plainly, right alongside the talk about His day. It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

I get why a crown comes to mind, but it's not the word here. Jesus says, "But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation." (Luke 17:25) Suffering and rejection come first. That's what He tells His disciples.

That would be a nicer sentence, friend, but it's not the one Jesus says. He says, "But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation." (Luke 17:25) The word is rejected. It's a hard one to read, and I think it's meant to be.

Ordinary life, right up to the last minute. Jesus says, "People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark." (Luke 17:27) Noah, the man who built the ark, was busy with a huge job while everyone else carried on with their day. Nothing in that list is strange, and that's the point of the picture.

That's a serious scene, but Jesus doesn't paint it here. He says, "People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark." (Luke 17:27) Dinner and weddings are what He names. Noah, the man who built the ark, is the one stepping inside.

Jesus never mentions anyone helping with the ark. What He says is, "People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark." (Luke 17:27) Noah is the man who built the ark. Those are the everyday things Jesus lists, so I'd stick to them.

Right on! Jesus says, "It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building." (Luke 17:28) Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5), lived in those days. That's a whole to-do list of regular life.

Jesus actually does say it. "It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building." (Luke 17:28) Lot was Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5). Buying, selling, planting and building are all right there in the verse.

That's the one. Jesus says, "But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all." (Luke 17:29) Sodom is the city Lot left. It's a heavy moment, and Jesus tells it plainly.

Those two do show up in the Bible, but in Egypt, not Sodom. Hail came down there (Exodus 9:23), and so did a thick darkness (Exodus 10:22). In Lot's story, Jesus says, "…fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all." (Luke 17:29)

Locusts are in the Bible, but they swarm over Egypt (Exodus 10:13), not Sodom. Jesus says Sodom got something different: "…fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all." (Luke 17:29) Sodom is the city Lot left that day.

This one's the reverse, friend. Jesus says, "On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions." (Luke 17:31) So the person up there stays up there and doesn't go grab anything first. I'd be tempted to run for my favorite mixing bowl, so I'm listening hard.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions." (Luke 17:31) He says not to go down for them. I'm not saying I wouldn't want my mixing bowl, but that's what He says.

Three little words, and they hit hard. Jesus says, "Remember Lot’s wife!" (Luke 17:32) Lot was just in the last verses, leaving Sodom, so His listeners had her story to think of. He doesn't say anything more about her here.
Noah is in this passage, so I see why you went there. But Jesus doesn't mention his wife anywhere. The line is "Remember Lot’s wife!" (Luke 17:32) Lot is the one whose story He had just told.
Abraham's family is close by, since Lot was his nephew (Genesis 12:5). But the wife Jesus names is a different one. He says, "Remember Lot’s wife!" (Luke 17:32) It's short, and it's meant to stick.

That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it." (Luke 17:33) It sounds backwards the first time through. I had to read it twice myself.

Regret would turn the verse sour, and Jesus doesn't say that. He says, "Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it." (Luke 17:33) The word is preserve. It's a surprising sentence, with the second half turning the first one on its head.

Forgetting doesn't show up in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it." (Luke 17:33) The word is preserve. It's a twisty line, and a good one to sit with.

Right, baker. Jesus says, "I tell you, on that night two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left." (Luke 17:34) Two people in the very same spot, and the paths split. The verse doesn't say more than that, so I won't either.

Healing shows up a lot in Jesus' ministry, but not in this verse. He says, "…two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left." (Luke 17:34) Taken is the word. Two people, one bed, and one is taken.

A warning would be handy, wouldn't it? But the word Jesus uses is different. He says, "…two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left." (Luke 17:34) One is taken, and the other is left.
